edge_108.relationship: Ginzburg’s intensive cases challenge automatic transfer between general categories and particular situations
edge_108.evidence_note: Intensive cases test the adequacy of aggregate categories and general accounts; they need not reject every generalization. His 1993 pp. 32–33 explain constructed categories and contextual inquiry; this critique coexists with a newly specified positive contribution to relational social history.

edge_165.relationship: Skinner explicitly credits Collingwood’s changing questions and question-and-answer logic
edge_165.evidence_note: A specific connection through Collingwood, not an assertion that the Cambridge School is idealist or derives from the entire historicist grouping. Complete interview answers 1 and 6 provide retrospective first-person reception evidence for Skinner’s early practice; he also stresses analytical philosophy and warns against tidy intellectual autobiography. This does not establish reception by every contextual historian or a Collingwood-to-Austin transmission. The 1969 article pp. 37–38 supplies contemporary explicit question/answer reception; pp. 50–51 also criticize a particular Collingwood inference, recorded as a separate critique.

edge_259.relationship: Ginzburg defends evidentiary inference while recognizing the constructed stages of historical research
edge_259.evidence_note: A contribution by a particular microhistorian, not a position required of every small-scale history. His 1993 p. 32 explicitly joins narrative experiment to opposition to skeptical textual reduction; earlier 1992 context remains.

edge_268.relationship: Ginzburg contests textual reduction while treating narrative form as part of historical research
edge_268.evidence_note: A specific intervention in the 1992 volume, not a rejection of every form of linguistic analysis by all microhistorians. The 1993 discussion explicitly names Ankersmit. It cannot stand for all microhistorians or all linguistic approaches.
edge_268.map_label: Ginzburg: narrative need not erase knowledge

edge_568.relationship: Levi develops a method for examining choices, norms and group formation through lives
edge_568.evidence_note: The complete 1989 essay accepts Bourdieu’s warning but emphasizes bounded room to act within contradictory norms. This methodological contribution coexists with the undirected comparison of biography and microhistory; it does not make all life writing microstoria.

edge_614.relationship: Skinner explicitly credits the Investigations in asking about historical language use
edge_614.evidence_note: Interview answer 6 recalls reading and discussing the work, connecting it to purposeful discourse and public intentions. This retrospective evidence concerns Skinner’s pre-2000 practice; it does not establish one philosophy shared by Pocock or all contextual historians. The 1969 article p. 37 directly cites Investigations §§43 and 79, adding contemporary primary evidence to the retrospective interview.

edge_619.relationship: Skinner criticizes Collingwood’s inference from identifying a problem to solving it
edge_619.evidence_note: Skinner (1969), pp. 50–51, argues that intelligible attempts may fail to solve their problems. This specific criticism coexists with his acknowledged question/answer resource; it does not reject all contextual interpretation or every historicist position. Collingwood’s original passage remains to be collated.

edge_620.relationship: Koselleck invokes Nietzsche on historically accumulated concepts resisting definition
edge_620.evidence_note: Futures Past, chapter 5, p. 85, explicitly quotes the difficulty of defining what has a history. This supports a particular conceptual resource, not a complete Nietzschean genealogy of conceptual history.
edge_620.map_label: Historical concepts and limits of definition

edge_621.relationship: Koselleck uses Weber’s legitimacy typology to distinguish analytical categories
edge_621.evidence_note: Futures Past, chapter 5, p. 92, discusses transformation of historical political vocabulary into a scientific category. This specific example does not establish Weber as a founding inspiration of the entire program; Olsen’s introduction note 9 explicitly disputes that larger genealogy.
edge_621.map_label: Weber’s typology as an analytical example

edge_707.relationship: Levi questions fixed cultural contexts in Geertz’s interpretive practice
edge_707.evidence_note: The 1985 essay criticizes textualization and explanatory circularity while praising Geertz’s skill. This is Levi’s specific intervention, not a verdict shared by every microhistorian.

edge_708.relationship: Levi challenges Darnton’s use of predetermined cultural frameworks
edge_708.evidence_note: The review targets The Great Cat Massacre’s interpretation of tales and the printers’ episode. Levi acknowledges his selective reading; neither all cultural history nor all microhistory speaks with one voice.

edge_732.evidence_note: Selected primary passages distinguish semantic inquiry from direct reduction to social structures.

political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.
political.representative_figures_and_works: Ranke is one major nineteenth-century root. Later examples: Lewis Namier, Charles Tilly, and Lynn Hunt’s Politics, Culture, and Class (1984). Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: Archives, government and religious authority
strands.focus: Ranke’s church/state inquiry and Cam’s medieval local institutions use historical records for different political problems; neither alone founded all source criticism.
strands.works: History of the Popes (1834–1836); Liberties and Communities in Medieval England (1944)

strands.title: Parliamentary connections and collective biography
strands.focus: Reconstruct actors’ social and political connections; the institutional focus raises questions about ideology and people excluded from parliamentary participation.
strands.works: The Structure of Politics at the Accession of George III (1929)

strands.title: Voters and competing group explanations
strands.focus: Benson tests class-centered interpretations against ethnic and religious voting patterns in New York; this is a local historical argument, not a universal electoral rule.
strands.works: The Concept of Jacksonian Democracy (1961)

strands.title: Radical ideas and popular political action
strands.focus: Compare religious radicalism, Chartist participation and colonial peasant insurgency without making one a derivative instance of another.
strands.works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972); The Chartists (1984); Elementary Aspects (1983)

strands.title: Rights movements and political inclusion
strands.focus: Sustained organization for women’s rights is part of political history; it is not merely an appendix to histories of officeholders. Scott’s studies of French feminists and the parity movement, known through her reviewers, examine claims to inclusion caught between the abstract individual and sexual difference.
strands.works: Century of Struggle (1959)

strands.title: Collective claims and governing work
strands.focus: Tilly connects performances and repertoires with state/economic change; Cooper asks how colonial labor categories govern social relations. Their regional units and explanations differ.
strands.works: The Contentious French (1986); Decolonization and African Society (1996)

strands.title: Political rhetoric, symbols and social identities
strands.focus: Hunt uses Geertz in an analysis of revolutionary authority and joins symbolic practices with the sociology of political actors.
strands.works: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984)

strands.title: Diplomacy, conflict and expansion
strands.focus: Narrative accounts of political choices differ from Williams’s interpretation of ideology, political economy and American expansion; diplomatic history contains disagreement.
strands.works: The Guns of August (1962); The King’s Peace and The King’s War; The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959)

strands.title: Radical milieus, hostile sources and disputed labels
strands.focus: Davis questions inherited Ranter accounts; Thompson defends a historical milieu; Scott stresses anachronism and Smith disputes both sides’ handling of evidence and theology. These are different positions, not an adjudicated consensus.
strands.works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972); “On the Rant” and correspondence (1987)

strands.title: Local government, record production and representation
strands.focus: Cam’s inquiry connects the making of records, local courts and parliamentary representation. Documentary criticism and inferences about ordinary lives remain distinct tasks.
strands.works: Cam, Studies in the Hundred Rolls (1921), Liberties and Communities (1944), “Stubbs Seventy Years after” (1948)

strands.title: Narrative, motives and contemporary uncertainty
strands.focus: Wedgwood reconstructs decisions without giving actors knowledge of their outcome. Woolrych also asks what this approach leaves unexplained about allegiance and regional differences.
strands.works: The King’s Peace (1955); The King’s War (1958), prefaces discussed by Woolrych (1998)

strands.title: Narrative synthesis and specialist collaboration
strands.focus: Tuchman’s account of producing A Distant Mirror identifies research, medieval advice and editing. These contributions support a synthesis whose event selection and explanatory claims remain open to criticism.
strands.works: A Distant Mirror (1978), acknowledgments and foreword

strands.title: Political ideas in different social situations
strands.focus: Wood questions applying Namier’s skepticism about ideas to revolutionary America. His reading of Bailyn connects changing beliefs with social circumstances and unintended outcomes; it does not make all political action a deliberate pursuit of abstract principles.
strands.works: Namier, “Human Nature in Politics” (1955/2000); Wood, “Rhetoric and Reality” (1966/1968), 69–78

strands.title: Press freedom and institutional dependence
strands.focus: Goldman traces how municipal protection, financing and censorship shaped political printing. Public controversy emerged through conflicts among editors and authorities, rather than automatically following a declaration of press freedom.
strands.works: “Libertad de imprenta” (2000), 10–15

strands.title: Public spaces and competing explanations
strands.focus: Goldman uses a plural account of public spaces. Sábato asks whether the collection’s cultural emphasis loses explanatory specificity and overlooks republican currents or differences among cases, while recognizing its comparative value.
strands.works: Los espacios públicos en Iberoamérica (1998); Goldman and Sábato (2000)

strands.title: The new political history of Britain, 1993–2011
strands.focus: After the Social History round on Stedman Jones (1992–93), British political history took the linguistic turn and argued with it. Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) held that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); his Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives'. Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin), and Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party' for the politics of place and gender; Vernon found it 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999) and Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined. Electing Our Masters (2009) followed the hustings and the platform; in 2011 Lawrence argued for a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Positions within one field, not a school; the debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: Vernon, Politics and the People (1993), ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996); Epstein, Radical Expression (1994); Lawrence and Taylor, eds, Party, State and Society (1997); Lawrence, Speaking for the People (1998), Electing Our Masters (2009), 'Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity' (2011); Vernon's review and Lawrence's response (Reviews in History, 1999/2010)

context.label: Contextual intellectual history / Cambridge School
context.description: Reads arguments as interventions in historically specific linguistic and political contexts. Skinner emphasizes what authors were doing in writing; Pocock reconstructs political languages. The Cambridge School is a grouping of related projects, not a uniform method or a synonym for every contextual history. Dunn joins philosophical precision to reconstructing historical acts; Laslett’s textual editing and later inquiries into rights extend the grouping without supplying one shared doctrine.

context.scope_note: Skinner’s interventions and Pocock’s political languages are related but not identical; the Cambridge School is narrower than all contextual interpretation. Public conventions constrain possible interventions; historical context is neither a complete causal deduction of a text nor recovery of a private intention without evidence. Later accounts dispute simple Laslett-to-Skinner founding narratives. Named philosophical resources are particular receptions, not school membership.

strands.title: Skinner’s philosophical resources
strands.focus: His retrospective account joins changing questions in Collingwood with language use in Wittgenstein and doing things with words in Austin. This records an acknowledged combination in Skinner’s work, not their doctrinal identity.
strands.works: On Encountering the Past (2002), answers 1 and 6 about earlier work

strands.title: Interventions, conventions and intended force
strands.focus: Skinner separates what words mean from what an author is doing with them. Public conventions and evidence constrain interpretation; a social setting alone does not determine the complete meaning of an intervention.
strands.works: Meaning and Understanding (1969), pp. 35–53

strands.title: Historically available levels of argument
strands.focus: Pocock asks at what level people actually formulated political ideas. A maximally coherent philosophical reconstruction and a history of thinking are legitimate but different inquiries; ideas remain historical events even when not the sole cause of action.
strands.works: The history of political thought: a methodological inquiry (1962), reprint pp. 3–11

strands.title: Republican fragility, virtue and corruption
strands.focus: Pocock’s introduction selects the problem of a republic’s existence in time, then proposes English and Atlantic continuations involving property, arms and commerce. It acknowledges Baron’s controversial resource and Skinner’s collaboration; this is a selected argument, not an exhaustive Atlantic narrative.
strands.works: The Machiavellian Moment (1975), introduction vii–x

strands.title: Philosophical precision and historical acts
strands.focus: Dunn distinguishes a proposition’s logical identity from a historical statement’s activity, including irony and polemic. Reconstructing the act requires evidence of the person’s available situation; philosophical and historical problems cannot simply replace one another.
strands.works: The Identity of the History of Ideas (1968), selected pp. 85–104

strands.title: Critical editions and disputed methodological succession
strands.focus: Laslett’s Locke edition and discussions with Dunn belong to contextual inquiry. They do not establish that Skinner inherited a complete method from him; Furuta’s later argument explicitly contests such a simple sequence.
strands.works: Two Treatises of Government, Laslett edition (1960); Dunn (1968); Furuta (2021), abstract

strands.title: Rights across philosophical and political contexts
strands.focus: Tuck traces natural-rights theories, Brett differentiates scholastic uses of ius, and Tully joins historical with critical inquiry around Locke. These projects extend the range of questions without forming one origin story; the present selections rely on scoped descriptions.
strands.works: Natural Rights Theories (1979); Locke in Contexts (1993); Liberty, Right and Nature (1997)

micro.label: Microhistory / everyday life
micro.description: Italian microstoria reconstructs relations and tests categories through close inquiry; German Alltagsgeschichte studies everyday practices and power. Neither is defined by small places alone, and their intellectual exchanges do not erase their differences.
micro.representative_figures_and_works: Carlo Ginzburg, The Cheese and the Worms (1976); Giovanni Levi; Alf Lüdtke. Natalie Zemon Davis: The Return of Martin Guerre (1983); Martin Broszat et al.: Bayern in der NS-Zeit (1977–83).

representative_people.context: Reconstructs Menocchio’s reading through inquisitorial records; later argues that narrative construction can coexist with evidentiary claims.
representative_people.works: The Cheese and the Worms (Italian 1976); “Microhistory: Two or Three Things That I Know about It” (1993)

representative_people.context: Reconstructs social relations and individual strategies at close range; Ginzburg’s account stresses their relation to wider contexts. His own methodological essays examine choices within conflicting norms and question fixed cultural contexts in interpretive history.
representative_people.works: Inheriting Power: The Story of an Exorcist (English 1988); I pericoli del geertzismo (1985); Les usages de la biographie (1989)

representative_people.context: Alltagsgeschichte researcher examining workers’ everyday practices, criticizing some structural priorities and drawing on Mann’s power networks.
representative_people.works: “Polymorphous Synchrony: German Industrial Workers and the Politics of Everyday Life” (1993)

representative_people.context: Examines occupational classification in Turin; Ginzburg identifies her relational reconstruction alongside Levi’s.
representative_people.works: La Ville et les métiers (1990)

representative_people.context: Microanalytical interlocutor whose formulation about exceptional evidence informs Ginzburg’s account of comparison.
representative_people.works: “Micro-analisi e storia sociale” (1977), discussed by Ginzburg (1993)

representative_people.context: Engages anthropology critically and collaboratively, including a working group with Lüdtke, Sabean and others.
representative_people.works: “Missionaries in the Row Boat”? (1987); with David Sabean, eds., Interest and Emotion (1984)

representative_people.context: Retrospective methodological interlocutor: Ginzburg praises his treatment of historical scale while explicitly denying known influence on microhistory’s emergence.
representative_people.works: History: The Last Things before the Last (1969), discussed by Ginzburg (1993), pp. 26–27

representative_people.context: An edited EHESS collection investigates changes of observational scale and generalization; it neither equates all small studies with microstoria nor makes small intrinsically superior. His own scale essay treats changed observation as changing the object and relationships available for analysis.
representative_people.works: Jeux d’échelles (editor, 1996); Micro-analyse et construction du social (1996)

representative_people.context: A critic of Alltagsgeschichte’s conceptual and explanatory claims who also acknowledges its cultural and experiential contributions.
representative_people.works: Alltagsgeschichte: Königsweg zu neuen Ufern oder Irrgarten der Illusionen? (1980s versions)

representative_people.context: Mexican local historian combining archives, conversations and lived experience for a local readership. This microhistoria is a distinct project, not a presumed branch of Italian microstoria.
representative_people.works: Pueblo en vilo (1968; revised edition consulted, 1979)

representative_people.context: González credits her corrections, proposed changes and preparation of the manuscript; the credited collaboration exceeds typing.
representative_people.works: Editorial collaboration on Pueblo en vilo, acknowledged in its preface

representative_people.context: Her preserved correspondence, association papers and long series of household accounts supplied González’s local history.
representative_people.works: Private archive and household expense notebooks used in Pueblo en vilo

representative_people.context: The Return of Martin Guerre (French 1982, the year of the film; English 1983) treats a village imposture. In ‘On the Lame’ (1988) she described her reconstruction from Coras, Le Sueur and the Parlement registers as a conjectural argument, and in 1997 she called her route ‘microhistory (or what I called ethnography) via film’. Finlay’s 1988 critique of its ‘invention’ and her reply are both recorded. Her cultural and women’s-history contexts remain.
representative_people.works: Le Retour de Martin Guerre (1982) and The Return of Martin Guerre (1983); “On the Lame” (AHR Forum, 1988)

representative_people.context: Led the Institut für Zeitgeschichte’s Bayern in der NS-Zeit project, a founding programme for the history of everyday life under National Socialism. His structuralist interpretation of the regime is a separate context.
representative_people.works: Bayern in der NS-Zeit (1977–1983), ed. with others

representative_people.context: Charges an ‘excess of invention’ in Davis’s portrait of Bertrande de Rols and insists on ‘the sovereignty of the sources’, while praising her portrait of peasant life; Davis replied in the same AHR Forum.
representative_people.works: “The Refashioning of Martin Guerre” (AHR Forum, 1988)

strands.title: Italian microstoria
strands.focus: A varied research programme connecting intensive cases to larger questions; cultural and social-relational inquiries overlap.
strands.works: Ginzburg (1976, 1993); Levi (English 1988); Cerutti (1990)

strands.title: Alltagsgeschichte
strands.focus: Lüdtke studies workers’ situated practices and power, using Mann as well as questioning structural priorities.
strands.works: “Polymorphous Synchrony” (1993); The History of Everyday Life (English 1995)

strands.title: Social relations and changing categories
strands.focus: Close reconstruction examines how relations and classifications are made through action.
strands.works: Levi, Inheriting Power; Cerutti, La Ville et les métiers

strands.title: Exceptional evidence and historical inference
strands.focus: An unusual case can expose assumptions without statistically representing a population.
strands.works: Ginzburg (1993), discussing Grendi (1977)

strands.title: History and anthropology in working exchange
strands.focus: Critical engagement with Cohn and collaborative research complicate a one-way borrowing model.
strands.works: Medick, “Missionaries in the Row Boat”? (1987)

strands.title: Moving between historical scales
strands.focus: Results at one scale cannot simply be transferred to another; retrospective affinity is distinguished from transmission.
strands.works: Ginzburg (1993), pp. 26–27, on Kracauer (1969)

strands.title: Everyday history, concepts and explanation
strands.focus: Wehler values the recovery of culture and experience but disputes claims to a replacement explanatory framework. Lüdtke challenges the reduction of everyday history to an illustrative supplement, while accepting some criticism of romanticization and insisting on reconstructing connections between traces. Both positions are internally qualified.
strands.works: Wehler, Alltagsgeschichte critique (1980s); Lüdtke, introduction (1989)

strands.title: Testing context through close interpretation
strands.focus: Levi argues that small episodes should revise the explanatory context, criticizing Darnton’s assumed cultural patterns while distinguishing Geertz’s accomplishments from mechanical applications.
strands.works: I pericoli del geertzismo (1985; Portuguese translation 1999)

strands.title: Choices within conflicting norms
strands.focus: Levi’s biography essay examines limited room for action and the formation of groups within contradictory normative systems; his disagreement with Bourdieu is one of emphasis.
strands.works: Les usages de la biographie (1989)

strands.title: Varying scale changes the object of inquiry
strands.focus: Revel distinguishes changes of analytical scale from merely magnifying an unchanged object; no scale has an automatic privilege. Relational inquiry makes collective formation a problem to explain.
strands.works: Micro-analyse et construction du social (1996), sections 3–4

strands.title: Mexican microhistoria and local readership
strands.focus: González explains local events alongside regional and national pressures, combining documentary records, informal conversations and personal recollection. His claims to typicality and his treatment of uncorroborated memory are methodological choices open to criticism.
strands.works: Pueblo en vilo (1968; revised edition 1979)

strands.title: Archives, informants and editorial collaboration
strands.focus: González’s preface credits Josefina’s archive, his father’s recollections, other informants and Armida’s revisions. These contributions make the local history a collaborative production despite its single-author title page.
strands.works: Pueblo en vilo, preface (consulted 1979)

strands.title: Reconstruction, invention and the sovereignty of sources
strands.focus: In ‘On the Lame’ (1988) Davis described her reconstruction of a village imposture from legal, notarial and printed records as conjectural, citing Ginzburg’s evidential paradigm; Finlay contests where reconstruction becomes invention, and Davis replies that the boundary was the book’s question. Both positions are recorded; neither settles the method.
strands.works: The Return of Martin Guerre (1982–83); Finlay and Davis, AHR Forum (1988)

micro.scope_note: Italian microstoria and German Alltagsgeschichte have distinct origins and aims; scale alone is not membership in either project. Evidence, narrative and generalization remain contested within this umbrella. Kracauer is a retrospective comparison, not a claimed founder. González’s Mexican microhistoria is included as a distinct local-history project; shared terminology does not establish transmission from Italian or German programmes.

conceptual.label: Conceptual history / Begriffsgeschichte
conceptual.description: Traces changing political and social concepts in relation to historical experience, conflict, and expectations. Koselleck links conceptual change to different temporalities and to the emergence of modern historical consciousness. This overlaps with contextual intellectual history while asking different questions about semantic change across time. Collective German lexicon work, French studies of polemical usages and Richter’s comparisons represent distinct programs. Concepts can register and help shape social processes without exhausting those processes.
conceptual.representative_figures_and_works: Reinhart Koselleck, Vergangene Zukunft (1979), translated as Futures Past (1985; Columbia edition 2004). The German conceptual-history tradition is related to, but not a branch of, Skinner and Pocock’s Cambridge School.

representative_people.context: German conceptual history; not a branch of the Cambridge School. Separates words from concepts, concepts from social reality and analytical categories from historical actors’ vocabulary; experience and expectation organize questions rather than determine their answers.
representative_people.works: Vergangene Zukunft (1979); Futures Past (1985)

representative_people.context: A coeditor of the German historical-concepts lexicon whose program differs from Koselleck’s. Tribe discusses criticism of his earlier völkisch framing and later revisions; original editions are not collated here.
representative_people.works: Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe, collective editorial project; discussion in Tribe’s Futures Past introduction (2004), pp. x–xiv

representative_people.context: A coeditor of the German lexicon with a distinct social-historical program; editorial collaboration does not establish one shared analytical method.
representative_people.works: Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe, collective editorial project; Koselleck’s preface and Tribe’s introduction to Futures Past

representative_people.context: Explicitly compares German conceptual history, the French Handbuch and Cambridge political-thought programs. The checked abstracts support comparative questions, not every judgment in the unread chapters.
representative_people.works: The History of Political and Social Concepts (1995), chapters 4 and 6, abstracts

representative_people.context: Coedits the French Handbuch and, with Gumbrecht, examines philosophe as a social role with competing pragmatic uses. This is a separate empirical program, not an unaltered copy of the German lexicon.
representative_people.works: Handbuch politisch-sozialer Grundbegriffe in Frankreich 1680–1820, Heft 3 (1985); with Gumbrecht, Philosophe, Philosophie, pp. 7–14

representative_people.context: Named coeditor of the 1985 French Handbuch volume. Editorial responsibility is documented; the checked preview does not establish sole authorship of its methodological article.
representative_people.works: Handbuch politisch-sozialer Grundbegriffe in Frankreich 1680–1820, Heft 3 (1985), title/imprint

representative_people.context: Coauthors the French study of philosophe, distinguishing changing social roles and pragmatic oppositions from dictionary definitions alone.
representative_people.works: With Rolf Reichardt, Philosophe, Philosophie (1985), selected pp. 7–14

representative_people.context: Koselleck explicitly invokes the difficulty of defining concepts that contain a history. This particular quotation does not establish adherence to Nietzsche’s entire philosophy.
representative_people.works: On the Genealogy of Morality (1887), quoted in Futures Past, chapter 5, p. 85

representative_people.context: Koselleck uses Weber’s legitimacy typology as an example of historical vocabulary becoming an analytical category. Olsen disputes a general Weber-based founding genealogy; the narrower example is preserved.
representative_people.works: Legitimacy typology discussed in Futures Past, chapter 5, p. 92

representative_people.context: Koselleck’s preface invokes the plurality of times as a resource for differentiating historical temporalities. This is a quoted resource, not a complete account of Herder’s history.
representative_people.works: Passage on plural times quoted in Koselleck’s preface to Futures Past, pp. 1–5

representative_people.context: Reconstructs competing uses of public opinion in constitutional argument; included for this practice without claiming membership in a German school.
representative_people.works: “Libertad de imprenta, opinión pública y debate constitucional” (2000), 15–20

conceptual.scope_note: Koselleck’s conceptual change and historical time differ from reconstructing a particular author’s intervention. Brunner, Conze and Koselleck’s editorial association does not imply identical methods or political commitments. Experience and expectation are formal research categories with variable contents; the proposed modern temporal transformation is neither a universal timetable nor a prediction of particular events.

strands.title: Words, concepts and overlapping semantic layers
strands.focus: The same word can persist while conceptual content changes; a concept can carry multiple historical layers. Koselleck combines synchronic usage with diachronic comparison without treating every word as a key historical concept.
strands.works: Futures Past, chapter 5, pp. 75–92

strands.title: Concepts as indicators and factors
strands.focus: Concepts register social relations and can help act upon them, but social events are not identical with their linguistic conceptualization. Historians must also distinguish actors’ terms from their own justified analytical categories.
strands.works: Futures Past, chapter 5, pp. 75–92

strands.title: Experience, expectation and unequal temporalities
strands.focus: These formal categories direct questions about remembered pasts and anticipated futures. Their asymmetry does not independently predict contents; Koselleck’s modernity thesis recognizes simplification, unequal social temporalities and recurring structures.
strands.works: Futures Past, preface and selected chapter 14 pp. 255–264, 271–275

strands.title: Collective lexicon, distinct programs and political criticism
strands.focus: Brunner, Conze and Koselleck participate in one editorial project with different research emphases. Criticism of Brunner’s political framing and textual revisions must be attributed and assessed through evidence, without assigning a uniform position to all editors and contributors.
strands.works: Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe; Koselleck’s preface and Tribe’s selected introduction

strands.title: French social roles and opposing uses
strands.focus: Gumbrecht and Reichardt investigate philosophe as a social role. Opponents can use similar semantic contents with opposed force; dictionaries participate in polemics instead of neutrally settling every usage. Their court discussion explicitly draws on Elias.
strands.works: Philosophe, Philosophie, Handbuch Heft 3 (1985), pp. 7–14

strands.title: Comparing conceptual history and political languages
strands.focus: Richter’s 1995 comparison makes differences among the German lexicon, French Handbuch and Skinner/Pocock programs explicit. Shared historical vocabulary questions do not establish one method or an origin of one school in another.
strands.works: The History of Political and Social Concepts (1995), chapters 4 and 6, abstracts

strands.title: Public opinion and contested sovereignty
strands.focus: Goldman distinguishes appeals to an enlightened general will from the divergent opinions of provinces. The meaning of public opinion changes within struggles over who can speak for a sovereign people.
strands.works: “Libertad de imprenta” (2000), 15–20; earlier joint presentation acknowledged in note 26
